summary: This Cleveland Clinic Health Library article explains how human hearing works, describing the outer, middle, and inner ear and the auditory nervous system that carries sound signals to the brain. It outlines a step-by-step hearing process, common causes of hearing loss such as aging, ear trauma, disease, medication, loud sound exposure, and earwax buildup, and advises when to see a hearing specialist. It also covers hearing tests, ways to protect hearing, and treatment options such as hearing aids and cochlear implants.
one_line: Cleveland Clinic article explaining how the ear and auditory system process sound, common causes of hearing loss, and how to protect hearing.
key_facts: The outer ear consists of the pinna and ear canal, and the pinna funnels sound into the ear canal like a reverse megaphone.
The middle ear contains the eardrum (tympanic membrane) and the ossicles: the malleus, incus and stapes.
The cochlea, a spiral-shaped structure in the inner ear, means snail shell and is lined with tiny hair cells.
The auditory nerve runs from the cochlea to a station in the brain stem known as the nucleus, and neural impulses then travel to the temporal lobe.
Visit a hearing care provider immediately for sudden hearing loss, even if it occurs in only one ear.
Seeking medical attention within the first 72 hours is essential to reduce the risk of complications, including permanent hearing loss.
Noise-induced hearing loss is described as 100% preventable by using hearing protection devices like earplugs or earmuffs.
Earwax (cerumen) is normal and healthy, but too much can block sound from reaching the eardrum and lead to hearing loss.
Cardiovascular diseases and diabetes can increase the risk for hearing issues by decreasing blood supply to the ear and auditory system.
Some medications, such as cancer treatment drugs, can contribute to hearing loss.
The article advises not to exceed 80% volume for more than 90 minutes a day when listening to music through headphones or earbuds.
A hearing test called an audiogram is given in a soundproof booth, where the patient presses a button when hearing a sound.
More than 37 million adults in the U.S. have some degree of hearing loss, according to the note from Cleveland Clinic.
Treatments and devices that can improve hearing include hearing aids, cochlear implants and bone anchored implants.
The article was last reviewed by a Cleveland Clinic medical professional on 02/21/2023.
